To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) the dual fluorophore calcium green 2 dye has two conformers in aqueous solution, (b) one of the conformers is fluorescent, and (c) single molecule photobleaching is due to the irreversible photodamage of a single fluorophore.

the fluorescence of the Ca(2+) ion indicator dye, Calcium Green 2, is quenched when bound as a nonemissive dimer and is enhanced when bound as a fluorescent monomer; the fluorescence of the dye is enhanced by a simple statistical increase of the number of fluorescent monomers in the presence of Ca(2+); and the photobleaching behavior of the dye is consistent with irreversible damage to one of the two fluorophores.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the spectroscopic properties of the Ca(2+) binding dye CG-2 are consistent with a model in which the dye exists in two distinct conformations, one of which is highly fluorescent and Ca(2+) bound, while the other exists as a highly quencher intramolecular dication dimer, which is Ca(2+) unbound.
the spectroscopic properties of CG-2 are consistent with those of a dual-fluorescent molecule that is capable of undergoing reversible intramolecular excitation energy transfer.
the fluorescence of CG-2 is due to a single fluorophore and that the other fluorophore is not involved in the fluorescence emission process.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the photophysical properties of CG-2 are consistent with a simple model of Förster coupling between chromophores in an extended conformation, but the single-molecule photophysical properties of this dye are complicated by the presence of an intramolecular dative bond that is broken upon Ca(2+) binding.

we have developed a model that can explain the ensemble and single molecule photophysics of CG-2, which can be used as a basis for understanding the spectroscopic properties of other dual-fluorochrome Ca(2+) indicators.

the dual-fluorochrome CG-2 dye is an excellent Ca(2+) probe for ensemble measurements, but the presence of two fluorophores in close proximity makes it an unsuitable Ca(2+) sensor for single molecule studies.
The main takeaway from our work is that
single-molecule spectroscopy can be used as a tool for the characterization of the conformational dynamics of complex fluorophores and the photophysics of their constituent fluorophores.
single-molecule spectroscopic measurements are essential for the complete characterization of a Ca(2+) dye, as the ensemble spectroscopic measurements alone are insufficient.
single molecule studies are a powerful tool for understanding the photophysical behavior of dyes and fluorophores in solution.
